title: When We Drift: One Name for Suffering
reflection: Name your own drift this week, kindly, as weather and not verdict. Is it the heavy shape or the fast shape? Then take the one small step that matches it: a little movement and light for the heavy, a few long out-breaths for the fast.

questions.q: What does Swamiji say anṛta is, and what it is not?
o: Not-Ṛta, a system drifted out of step with the rhythms it lives in; not a judgement of weak or lazy people.
A kind of wrongdoing, for which a person is held to account by others and by his own conscience.
A rare illness that a doctor can find by one test and then treat by a course of known medicine.
A habit of speaking falsely, which a person can give up at once by deciding to give it up.
questions.e: A system can drift through no fault of its own. The modern world pours light into the night, shatters attention, offers food at every moment, swaps familiar faces for strangers and speeds past what a nervous system can recover from. Drift is close to the baseline, not the exception.
questions.c: Anṛta is structural drift, not a failing

questions.q: “A symptom such as anxiety or exhaustion is evidence that a person is doing life wrong.”
questions.e: It is often evidence of a responsive, working system accurately registering the pressure of a world that has itself drifted from fit; a sane response of a healthy instrument to an ill-fitting environment. So we meet the symptom with curiosity, not blame.
questions.c: A symptom can be a sane response

questions.q: A woman rests but wakes unrefreshed, with a low hum of anxiety under a perfectly fine day. How does Swamiji read this?
o: As everyday faces of one state, a system out of fit, held lightly as weather and not as a verdict.
As a sign of poor character, which she can put right by a firmer resolve to look on the bright side.
As an illness she must hide from others until it has passed, since talking of it would make it worse.
As nothing of note, since all adults feel this way and it would be unwise to give it a name at all.
questions.e: The lesson names everyday faces: tiredness sleep does not cure, sleep that does not restore, an objectless hum, hunger eating does not satisfy, activity that drains, the treadmill feeling, a harsh inner critic, and relationships that feel like unaffordable work. Not one is a personal failing.
questions.c: These are faces of one drift, held as weather

questions.q: Kai asks whether a good life is one with no struggle. What does Swamiji say?
o: No: a fitted life still meets difficulty, but with resources, and recovers between the rounds.
Yes: once a person is in fit the struggle ends, and a life that still has struggle is not yet fitted.
No: struggle is the only mark of a good life, so a person should look for all the difficulty he can.
Yes: struggle is always a sign of drift, so it ought to be put out of one’s life as soon as it begins.
questions.e: Vivekananda was blunt that life is struggle, and when it stops, so does life. Drift is not the presence of difficulty but meeting it without resources and taking damage each cycle, never recovering before the next blow. A fitted life still gets cut; it just is not bleeding from a hundred old wounds.
questions.c: Fit means resources and recovery, not no struggle

questions.q: Why are there exactly two shapes of drift, in the three-strand picture?
o: The still centre is too weak to hold the proportion, so either form or movement takes over.
The body can only fail in two ways, which are to be too fast or too slow, and nothing else.
Two kinds of people exist, the active and the quiet, and each has a drift of the matching kind.
Day and night each give a drift, so that the shape depends on the time at which it occurs.
questions.e: Too much form and not enough movement is the heavy shape: the system over-consolidates and stalls. Too much movement and not enough centre is the fast shape: it oscillates and cannot settle. Two opposite shapes, one direction of return: rebuild the centre.
questions.c: Weak centre lets form or movement take over

questions.q: A man feels heavy and stalled, and cannot move even for things he cares about. Which reading and first step fit?
o: Heavy drift: reintroduce movement, light and rhythm, gently, and do not demand that he perform.
Fast drift: give him a still axis, a slow breath, and demand a firm routine from him as well.
A lack of will, so he should be told to try harder, since willpower is what raises a person.
A passing fault, so he should be left to himself until the heaviness has gone of its own accord.
questions.e: Willpower cannot raise the fallen, any more than shouting can raise a fallen horse; the still centre that would lift him is what is depleted. Try harder is the cruellest advice for that state. For the fast drift the repair is the opposite: give the spinning system something to hold still.
questions.c: Heavy drift needs movement, light and rhythm

questions.q: Kai’s midnight-phone loop keeps him awake, each step feeding the next. What does Swamiji ask him to do?
o: Map it as fast drift and break it at exactly one point, the easiest, and watch it loosen.
Give up the phone altogether from tonight, since any loop of this kind can be broken only by force.
Blame himself firmly each night, since shame is what will make him put the phone down at last.
Wait for the loop to stop of itself, since a pattern of this kind needs only time and no change.
questions.e: Phone by the bed, wrecked sleep, morning fatigue, caffeine, afternoon crash, evening dread, and back to the phone. Naming the structure lets him interrupt it with less self-blame and more precision: it is a system and not a lecture about his character.
questions.c: Map the loop and cut it at one point

questions.q: Sarah asks whether a person who meditates a great deal and withdraws from life is in heavy drift. What test does Swamiji give?
o: Is this person becoming more alive to their life, or quietly disappearing from it? Real practice tends to more life.
Does the person meditate for long hours each day? A great many hours is itself the sign of drift.
Does the person say that he is happy? A person who says he is happy cannot be in heavy drift.
Does the person talk about practice? A person who talks of it is always showing a falling disengagement.
questions.e: Genuine practice raises a person, making them clearer, steadier and more available. They lose interest in idle stimulation as one outgrows food that no longer nourishes: a rising disengagement. The heavy drift is a falling disengagement, vitality dimming. Same surface, opposite direction.
questions.c: Rising disengagement frees; falling withdrawal shuts in

questions.q: How does Conversation 4.7 read the opening of the Bhagavad Gītā?
o: As mixed drift: Arjuna collapses, and Krishna diagnoses drift from the Self and gives four paths back.
As a battle story, which has nothing to do with the state of the human mind or of its health.
As a call to arms, in which Krishna tells Arjuna to fight and to put every doubt out of his mind.
As a legend of a god, which only shows what a human being cannot hope to do for himself.
questions.e: Arjuna’s trembling, parched mouth and dropped bow read as acute autonomic dysregulation, a panic tipping toward shutdown. Krishna does not say leave or calm down; he names the drift from the deepest Self and gives four paths: knowledge, devotion, action and meditation. All turn the mind from pravṛtti toward nivṛtti.
questions.c: The Gītā opens with mixed drift and a course of return

questions.q: “In drift, measures such as heart-rate variability and the stress-hormone curve flatten or go incoherent, and every one of them is recoverable: drifted, not broken.”
questions.e: Dr Watson lists them: variability going jittery or flat, the daily hormone curve stuck high or never rising, the body clock desynchronised. Each is loss of resonant coherence becoming measurable, and each returns when the conditions are restored. Drift, unlike breakage, has a way home.
